title: AI "learned" that it can run my game headless in a Linux container and check the logs to see what happened...
author: EC36339
selftext:
... and the headless run part was by design.

What wasn't is that a coding agent analyzes what happened in the game with such a crude and token intensive tool as logs.

The agent needs better tools to read game state, and maybe influence the game, too.

So I need ideas. Who has done similar things, and what worked?

An LLM is obviously too slow to play a game in real time. But it doesn't have to. It could theoretically ...

1. Generate a map and let NPCs do stuff or fight each other (Easy. My coding agents already do that without being asked. Yesterday it built a "shooting range" for NPCs, and I only discovered it by accident. Found bugs, too, that the AI missed, because of course)

2. Script an NPC to do certain things

3. Control an NPC, not in real-time, but by "checking in with it" every so or ao many frames, reading out some kind of history and giving it new objectives.

All assuming that the game and engine supports it, and there is an interface an external agent can use and that goes both ways.

Oh, and of course you can pace the game loop with a fake clock, so the AI can run it for, say, 500 frames at, say, fake 60 hz as fast as the CPU allows, then pause it, read out game state, reason about it for as long as it takes, resume the game.

Another interface or data format that may be better than logs can be replicated state. If a game has multiplayer with state replication, just repurpose thr netcode to feed game state to an LLM (maybe via something intermediate that accumulates some high frequency data into some kind of short history or whatever).

Crazy ideas. But we live in crazy times, and trying out stupid ideas and failing is cheap now.

comments.author: Intelligent-Cap-8886
comments.body: Have you tried explaining the problem and asking for better logs?

replies.author: EC36339
replies.body:
That's oversimplifying it a bit, and general prompts like this usually give you garbage.

Besides, AI is quite good already at improving logs and will do so without even being asked, so that's covered.

It's logs as a tool in general that isn't good enough.

comments.author: Jealous-Store-4746
comments.body:
I've been co developing a fighting game with Astra and it's been a trip.  It does headless tests all the time and observes the different states that it cant test just by numbers and frame data. 
It chews through tokens but I'm mostly just doing it for fun on a plus account. It is silly what it can do

comments.author: Ok-File-2759
comments.body: Just create an mcp for your game

replies.author: EC36339
replies.body: Yeah, that was the idea. Still need to wrap my head around what an MCP actually is and does, but this may be the final opportunity to learn exactly that by doing.

comments.author: EchoingAngel
comments.body: My game makes a light weight factory as the start screen background and that tech was usable for Astra to run mass simulations of the game to refine different mechanics. It's been very useful, though be mindful, I've already found it cheating before (and that it cheated a week ago and I only now found out)

comments.author: UnderStrangeStars
comments.body:
That's really cool. As a non-AI developer, I do this for my game as well. Though that's because I work with other people for building a lot of the graphical front end, so as the developer I work in my lil headless backend simulation. The other benefit is that it can be engine agnostic - godot, unity, unreal, whatever! you just need bridges from the backend simulation to the deterministic rendered front end.

Anyways, now the less fun news -- maybe LLM is better at it than I am - but it's REALLY hard to program a bot that plays like a human. I usually just build out enough tests to make sure certain pathways, actions, etc are protected from soft locking a game session, and to have automated tests are save / resume states.

If you balance / tune your game around how an LLM builds a CPU player -- your players may not enough playing it. You must tune for humans.

replies.author: EC36339
replies.body:
So far the main benefit I see of putting an LLM into this loop is that it can reason very fast about data.

It replaces hours of juggling Excel sheets, parsing logs, and Python scripting.

About the no-softlock testing: I'm working on an algorithm thay builds abstract dungeons as graphs using a context free graph grammar. That's a separate project, though, not integrated into the game, yet.

It was a test in how well AI can formalise a mathematical algorithm and prove its correctness. I came up with the algorithm myself, but it had gaps and flaws (I didn't know it had flaws, except that it wasn't fleshed out and fullly thought through, which was the idea of the test). I let the AI fill the gaps, do the proofs and write tests (one generator, and one solver using Dijkstra's algorithm that simulates all the player's possible moves).

It took a few iterations to get right, and I have yet to feed the output into something that builds actual dungeon geometry, which is another hard problem to solve. If it turns out useful, I might make it open source.

comments.author: Short_Stable2397
comments.body:
Yes it's very possible. You haven't mentioned which engine you use though.

In case you use Godot or consider using it. What you're describing fits very well with [the MCP I built for Godot](https://asymptopia.dev/gdmaestro/). The agent will boot up the game, change state, inspect logs, send inputs to drive the game frame by frame. With a vision capable model the agent will also proactively take screenshots as evidence when implementing features or debugging.

replies.author: EC36339
replies.body:
I'm not using any engine.

If MCP is the protocol for this, I'll probably have to build an MCP.

comments.author: HitMePat
comments.body: Your LLM should be writing python scripts to play the game, not actually responding to real time events in the game and then burning tokens to figure out it's next move.  It knows the whole game loop.  It can play it without actually "playing" it.

comments.author: egonosz
comments.body:
Crazy ideas indeed, it called scenario tests and it is done for very long time in tech. 

Basically you want to have a way to save an initial state maybe commands too what you can apply runtime and pass and fail conditions. After this you can run different scenarios as tests automatically and deterministically or your ai.
